BI-RADS Category 4 covers a likelihood of malignancy that is above 2% and below 95% [2]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, a category 4B result indicates moderate suspicion for malignancy, which corresponds to a chance of cancer above 10% and up to 50% [1]. If a benign biopsy result is obtained with this category, it requires careful correlation with the imaging to determine whether it is concordant [1].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, the radiologist who performed the biopsy is responsible for determining concordance, documenting it, and communicating it [3]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, in a large study of non-palpable, non-calcified, circumscribed solid masses followed with mammography, 19 out of 1,403 masses, which is 1.4%, proved to be malignant [1]. This figure applies specifically to that group rather than to every circumscribed mass [1].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, a lobular shaped mass is a term from the 4th edition used in the UCI data to describe a mass with an undulating contour [1]. The 5th edition of BI-RADS removed this term, but the BI-RADS v2025 update brought it back as "lobulated," which is defined as a mass with one or more indentations creating an undulating contour [1]. Lobulated masses are typically benign, though they are viewed as slightly more suspicious than oval masses [1]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, an irregular mass is defined as a shape that is neither round, oval, nor lobulated [1]. An irregular shape is considered a suspicious feature; in one series of biopsied lesions, 73% of irregular masses were found to be malignant [1]. Furthermore, an irregular, spiculated, and high-density mass is characteristic of a classic BI-RADS category 5 finding [1][2], which indicates a likelihood of malignancy of 95% or greater [2].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, an iso-dense mass (also described as "equal density" in current terminology) is a mass that has the same attenuation as fibroglandular tissue [1]. On its own, having an iso-dense mass neither indicates nor excludes malignancy [1]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Fine needle aspiration is a minimally invasive procedure where a thin needle is used to draw cells from a mass so they can be examined under a microscope (cytological examination) [1]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

A benign biopsy result is reliable only when it agrees with the imaging findings, a concept known as concordance [1][2]. This is because pathology results must be carefully compared with the initial imaging to ensure they align and accurately reflect the tissue sampled [1][2]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Nuclear features describe the cell nuclei seen under a microscope in digitised fine needle aspiration images [1][2]. These features include radius, texture, perimeter, area, smoothness, compactness, concavity, concave points, symmetry, and fractal dimension [2]. In the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset, there are 30 such nuclear features, which consist of 10 distinct measurements summarized by their mean, standard error, and worst value [1][2].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Sensitivity is the share of people with the disease whom a test correctly flags, calculated as true positives divided by all people with the disease [1]. 

Specificity is the share of people without the disease whom the test correctly clears, calculated as true negatives divided by all people without it [1]. 

Screening programmes trade sensitivity and specificity against each other, and the majority of women recalled after a screening mammogram do not have cancer [1].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, digital breast tomosynthesis (also known as 3D mammography) differs from a regular 2D mammogram in the following ways:

* **Image Capture:** Regular mammograms take X-rays of the compressed breast in two views [2]. In contrast, digital breast tomosynthesis takes multiple low-dose X-ray exposures from several different angles [1][2].
* **Reconstruction:** Tomosynthesis reconstructs thin slices through the breast tissue, which helps reduce the overlap of tissue that can hide or mimic masses on standard 2D images [1][2].
* **Detection:** This technique improves cancer detection for many women with dense breasts [1].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, about 10% of US screening mammograms result in a recall for additional imaging [3]. Most women who are recalled after a screening mammogram do not have cancer [1]; specifically, only about one in twenty recalled women has cancer [3]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, the Dutch DENSE trial showed that offering MRI to women with extremely dense breasts after a normal mammogram reduced the rate of interval cancers from 5.0 down to 2.5 per 1,000 women invited (and 0.8 per 1,000 among those who were actually screened) [1]. However, this benefit came with a trade-off, resulting in approximately 80 false-positive results for every 1,000 MRI screens performed [1].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, neither ultrasound nor MRI can reliably show microcalcifications [1][2]. Specifically, MRI does not show microcalcifications [1], and ultrasound also cannot reliably show them [2].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, while the majority of certain suspicious features like spiculated masses are malignant (81%), a minority turn out to be benign [1]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Screening results can cause measurable distress [1]. Specifically, a Danish cohort study found that six months following a false-positive mammogram, women reported alterations in their existential values and inner calmness that were just as significant as those reported by women diagnosed with breast cancer [1]. Furthermore, three years after a false-positive result, these women continued to report more negative psychosocial consequences compared to women who received a normal result [1]. To help reduce this harm, clear and timely communication along with a short wait time for follow-up tests are important [1].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Cultural background affects breast screening communication in several ways: screening participation and the perception of risk vary across different cultural backgrounds, and language barriers can impact how results are understood [1]. Additionally, cultural beliefs about cancer can influence a person's willingness to participate in screening or pursue treatment [1]. To address these challenges, it is recommended to use culturally appropriate materials and professional interpreters rather than family members when needed [1].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

A normal mammogram result should be explained as reassuring, though it does not completely rule out cancer [1]. Mammography typically finds approximately 80% to 87% of cancers that are present, with fewer detected in dense breasts [1]. When communicating normal results, it is also important to encourage continued screening at the recommended intervals and to prompt the prompt review of any new symptoms [1]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, breast cancer is most frequently diagnosed between the ages of 65 and 74, with a median age at diagnosis of 64 [3]. Most breast cancers are generally diagnosed after age 50 [2]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, the four ACR BI-RADS breast density categories are:

* **Category A:** Almost entirely fatty, which applies to about 10% of women [1].
* **Category B:** Scattered areas of fibroglandular density, found in about 40% of women [1].
* **Category C:** Heterogeneously dense, present in about 40% of women [1].
* **Category D:** Extremely dense [1].

Nearly half of all women aged 40 and older who undergo mammograms have dense breasts, falling into either category C or D [1]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, after a person has breast cancer in one breast, the risk of developing a new cancer in the other breast is approximately 0.4% per year [1]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, the SEER program estimates about 322,000 new cases of female breast cancer in the United States in the year 2026 [1].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

The 1.7% five-year risk of invasive breast cancer threshold (calculated using the Gail model at age 35 or over, or an imaging-based model) is used by NCCN increased-risk recommendations to guide screening practices, specifically indicating the need for annual mammography with tomosynthesis and the consideration of annual MRI [2]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, the American Cancer Society (ACS), along with other US bodies, agrees that average-risk women should have regular screening mammography starting from their forties [1]. Additionally, for women with an elevated lifetime risk of about 20–25% or greater, the ACS recommends annual MRI screening along with mammography [2]. For women with a lifetime risk below 15%, the ACS recommends against MRI screening, and it considers the evidence insufficient for those with a lifetime risk between 15% and 20% [2]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, the Gail model should not be used for:
* Known mutation carriers [1].
* Women with a history of breast cancer [1].
* Women with ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) [1].
* Women who have had chest radiation [1].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, endocrine therapy is mentioned in the context of hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative disease. Specifically, CDK4/6 inhibitors are standard when combined with endocrine therapy for advanced disease [1]. Additionally, for hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer, endocrine therapy alone is utilized, and studies such as TAILORx evaluated outcomes for women receiving endocrine therapy alone compared to adding chemotherapy based on recurrence scores [3]. 

However, the provided documents do not contain information regarding the duration ("for how long") of endocrine therapy [1][2][3][4].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

The provided documents do not contain information about how ductal carcinoma in situ is treated. They only mention that mammography can detect microcalcifications as an early sign of ductal carcinoma in situ [1] and that low-grade ductal carcinoma in situ accounts for a large share of overdiagnosis in screening [2]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, the goal of treatment for Stage IV (metastatic) breast cancer is to control the disease and preserve quality of life for as long as possible, as a cure is rare [1]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Based on the provided documents, there is no mention of World Health Organization (WHO) screening recommendations for any specific age group. The provided documents outline screening recommendations from NCCN and ACS [1][2][3], but do not contain information covering WHO guidelines. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

Overdiagnosis refers to detecting a cancer that would never have caused symptoms during a woman's lifetime [1]. 

Regarding how common it is, estimates vary widely depending on the method used, ranging from under 10% to over 50% of screen-detected cancers [1]. For instance, the UK Independent Review in 2012 estimated that about 19% of cancers found through screening are overdiagnosed, which represents roughly 11% of all cancers diagnosed in women who were invited for screening [1]. Low-grade ductal carcinoma in situ makes up a large portion of these cases [1]. Additionally, screening programs carried out without adequate capacity to diagnose and treat findings can lead to harms such as overdiagnosis and overtreatment [2].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO) framework, the interval from first presentation to the start of treatment should be as short as possible [1]. Treatment should ideally start within about a month of diagnosis, with no more than approximately 90 days passing from the first appearance of symptoms to the start of treatment [1].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

BreastCare AI is a research and educational prototype that estimates the probability that a breast mass is malignant using four values: the patient's age and three BI-RADS descriptors (shape, margin, and density) [2]. 

It was trained on the UCI Mammographic Mass dataset, which is a public collection of 961 masses (831 with complete descriptors) gathered from a single German radiology institute between 2003 and 2006 [2]. The estimate is generated by a statistical model chosen by a fixed rule from a logistic regression and two LightGBM candidates [2]. 

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

When the estimated malignancy probability is 65% or higher, the app displays an enhanced high-risk notice [1]. 

A high estimate does not mean a diagnosis of cancer [1]. Instead, it means that masses sharing the same descriptors were frequently malignant in the training data [1]. 

Only a biopsy, examined by a pathologist, can confirm or exclude malignancy [1]. None of the outputs provided by the tool constitute a diagnosis [2].

⚕️ These findings must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any decision is made.

If you are feeling overwhelmed, you can contact your local emergency number or a crisis line [1]. In the US, you can call or text 988, in the UK and Ireland you can call Samaritans on 116 123, and elsewhere you can visit findahelpline.com to find free helplines [1].
